chapter: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
title: The varied sounds of New York clubs and the one-rose bar
summary: Hodes describes the distinct sounds on 52nd Street from Barney Bigard to Billie Holiday and Hot Lips Page. He also mentions the Ryan's Dixieland crowd.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And really appreciated what they did as a band. New York at that time, you could hear various sounds. You could walk down 52nd Street and see Barney Bigard playing with a small group at the Onyx. Across the street you could see Billie Holiday, you could see John Kirby with a band, Red -- I mean, Hot Lips Page. Everybody had their own little thing, Coleman Hawkins. There was no copying, like. And Jimmy Ryans and Dixieland, with Jack Teagarden or George Brunis or that sort of sound, what they called Dixieland. Tailgate, you know.

But each distinct and each mixing and each meeting at the corner bar, or the White Rose and we called it -- the One Rose and we called it the White Rose or the One Rose. And we all -- because you could get that double for ten cents more. A shot was 30, a double was 40.
Well, again, that's what we were talking about earlier, you know, about brotherhood of jazz musicians, that doesn't exist --
